claims.claim: Group-by sum and mean over 10M rows: pandas 3.0.6 0.22 s, Polars 1.44.2 0.11 s, DuckDB 1.5.5 0.06 s (best of 3, 4 cores).
claims.source: Measured in this repository's dev environment.

concept_html:
All four tools answer the same questions. Pick by where the data lives and how big it is next to your memory, not by fashion.

A measurement from this course's build: a group-by with sum and mean over 10 million rows and 1,000 groups, best of three runs on a 4-core machine. pandas 3.0.6 took 0.22 s, Polars 1.44 took 0.11 s, DuckDB 1.5 took 0.06 s. At this size every tool is fast enough. The choice matters when data outgrows memory.

Situation Good default
Data fits comfortably in memory, you need the scikit-learn, statsmodels or plotting ecosystem pandas
Files larger than you want in memory, heavy transforms, one machine Polars lazy (scan_parquet)
SQL is the clearest way to express it, or you join many files ad hoc DuckDB
Data already in a lakehouse, or larger than one machine, or a scheduled production job Spark (Track A)

The tools share the Apache Arrow memory format, so you mix them at the boundaries:

lazy_result = pl.scan_parquet("extracts/*.parquet").filter(...).group_by(...).agg(...)
summary = lazy_result.collect().to_pandas()     # Polars to pandas for statsmodels
rel = con.sql("SELECT ... FROM read_parquet('extracts/*.parquet')")
top = rel.pl()                                   # DuckDB to Polars

Rules for mixing:

  • Reduce first, convert last. Filter and aggregate in the engine that reads the files. Convert the small result.
  • Watch the index. Polars has no index. pl.from_pandas(df) drops a pandas index unless you pass include_index=True, or call reset_index() first.
  • Check dtypes after each hop. Text becomes str in pandas 3 and String in Polars. Nullable integers need care in both directions.

One project, one primary engine. A second tool at a clear boundary is fine. Four tools in one function is not.

lines: import pandas as pd
import polars as pl
def brand_totals(path_glob: str, wave: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Weight per brand for one wave, as pandas for modelling. Grain: one row per brand."""
pl.scan_parquet(path_glob)
.filter(pl.col("wave") == wave)
.agg(total=pl.col("weight").sum())

wrong_answers.feedback: pandas loads the whole selection into memory first. 40 GB does not fit in 16 GB.

exercises.fix_solution:
import polars as pl


def wave_mean(path: str, wave: str) -> float:
    """Mean weight for one wave."""
    result = (
        pl.scan_parquet(path)
        .filter(pl.col("wave") == wave)
        .select(pl.col("weight").mean())
        .collect()
        .item()
    )
    return float(result)
fix_solution_lines: import polars as pl
def wave_mean(path: str, wave: str) -> float:
"""Mean weight for one wave."""

.filter(pl.col("wave") == wave)
.select(pl.col("weight").mean())

wrong_answers.feedback: 50,000 rows fit in memory many times over. Spark adds start-up time and a cluster for no gain.
Pulling lakehouse tables into one pandas process moves the data away from the compute that already sits next to it.
pandas would load most of 25 GB into 32 GB of RAM. A lazy scan keeps memory in check.

title: Choosing pandas, Polars, DuckDB or Spark
why_html:
An analyst sets respondent_id as the pandas index to deduplicate, then hands the frame to a Polars function for a fast join. pl.from_pandas drops the index. The join key is gone, so the analyst joins on row position with hstack. Two waves sorted differently, and 11% of respondents got another person's scores.

pl.from_pandas(df.reset_index()) keeps the ID as a column, and the join uses it.
